title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: Underwriting Rule: a company's past is not the story it tells about itself; it is the sequence of decisions its cash flow made possible.
epigraph.author: Research Desk house maxim

web_blocks.html: Start with the registration certificate, because it tells you what kind of company this is. MPS Limited carries corporate identity number L22122TN1970PLC005795 [1]. It was incorporated in 1970 as the Indian subsidiary of Macmillan (Holdings) Limited. For its first four decades it was a captive that served the group owning it [3]. Macmillan, a UK publisher founded in 1843, reached India in 1892. In 1976 the former British prime minister Harold Macmillan inaugurated a publishing-services division in Bangalore. It was long known as the Information Processing Division and provided editorial and production services to international book and journal publishers [3]. In 2004 the company added a wholly owned technology subsidiary, MPS Technologies, for digital-publishing work. A later demerger separated domestic Indian publishing, which stayed as Macmillan Publishers India, from the services-and-technology business that became MPS [3].

Two corrections to the commissioning brief belong here. First, the shares did not list in 2007. The annual report states they have been listed since 10 December 2001 on BSE and 21 January 2002 on NSE [1]. The company was renamed from Macmillan India to MPS in 2009 [4]. Second, I could not verify the label 'publishing's first outsourcing vendor' from any source I read. The record does support a narrower claim. MPS has sold offshore editorial and production capacity to Western publishers since the 1970s, which is a durable enough claim.

The second origin story is 2011. ADI BPO Services Limited, a Delhi business-services firm led by Nishith Arora, bought Macmillan's stake in MPS and took management control [5, 6]. The company itself dates the change of majority stake to '2011-12' [3]. That holding company is still the promoter. It owns 1,16,90,615 of 1,71,05,816 shares, or 68.34%. The holding was unchanged at the 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026 balance-sheet dates [1]. The quarterly shareholding table shows 68.34% in every quarter from December 2023 to September 2026 [7]. I verified the share count in the audited note. I did not verify any family relationship between the promoter and the CEO, Rahul Arora. Mr Arora did tell the Q2 FY25 call he could answer 'from a promoter perspective and an MPS perspective' [8].

The holding structure has its own history. In 2017-18 the board proposed merging ADI BPO into MPS to remove a layer of holding company. A trade-press critic called it a regulatory tidy-up whose costs would fall on MPS [6]. The scheme was withdrawn in December 2018 [9]. The board revived it on 18 July 2025 [1]. The CEO told the Q1 FY26 call that the merger “will simplify the shareholding structure, enhance operational flexibility and strengthen direct promoter alignment” [10]. He added that this would be “all without affecting public shareholding” [10]. On 22 August 2026 the court-convened shareholders' meeting approved the scheme. All 1,16,90,615 promoter votes and all 5,51,213 institutional votes were in favour. Public non-institutional holders cast 1,52,327 votes for and 50 against [11]. The company's scheme page lists a tribunal second-motion order dated 16 September 2026. I have not read it, so final sanction is unconfirmed [9].

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited timeline, 1970 to November 2026: event and what changed economically
web_blocks.takeaway: Read the right-hand column as the story. The business changed economic species three times. It began as a captive production arm (1970-2011). It became a US-and-Europe content roll-up with a platform sideline (2013-2020). It is now a three-market knowledge company whose margin depends on AI-assisted delivery and recurring contracts (2022-2026). Each transition was financed from internal cash, with one exception: the FY15 raise.

web_blocks.html: From 2013 the engine was acquisition, and the record is checkable. The company counts 'eleven acquisitions in thirteen years' [1]. I could price six of them from primary documents. Five carry no disclosed price in anything I read: Element, EPS, Mag+, THINK and HighWire. The table sets out what is verifiable and what the later record says about each. The pattern is the one the CEO described on the Q2 FY25 call. Look for a business with an obvious fix, and fix it fast. He called AJE “MPS 2.0” in that sense [8].

web_blocks.caption: Acquisition ledger: what MPS paid, what it bought, and what the audited record shows afterwards
web_blocks.takeaway: Total identified consideration for the four priced deals since FY22 (EI Design, Liberate, AJE, Unbound) is about Rs 322 Cr. I computed it by adding 42.09, 70.33, 69.67 and 140.40. Compare that with the Rs 460 Cr paid out to shareholders in FY22-FY25 alone. MPS has been a high-distribution company that acquires, not a company that raises money to acquire. Goodwill reached Rs 376.32 Cr at 31 March 2026, which is 40% of total assets [1]. That is the price of the strategy. The purchases must keep earning their way.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: What a captive's DNA does to a collector
paragraphs: A captive learns to be low-cost and reliable because its parent always has an outside quote in the drawer. It does not learn to be chosen. MPS's history is the process of acquiring, one deal at a time, the skills a captive never needed. Those skills are selling, saying no to a bad contract, and deploying its own capital.

The pattern repeats in the numbers. The two largest purchases by revenue pulled operating margin down. FY19 fell to 26% after Tata Interactive. FY25 fell to 29% with AJE, which was loss-making when acquired [15]. Each repair pushed margin back up. The CEO described the trade-off on the Q2 FY25 call. He said “typically you have to chase one of these two things”: improve the margin profile, or chase growth [8]. Our judgment: that is the honest summary of this business. Margin and growth have almost never been maximised in the same year. So H1 FY27's combination (revenue +17.8%, margin 34.3%) is the thing to test, not assume [2].

web_blocks.html: Now the business cycle, from the price-blind snapshot of the consolidated accounts [7]. I computed every figure here with Python from the snapshot's sales, operating profit and net profit rows. The annual reports prevail where they differ, and they differ only at the rounding margin. Over FY15 to FY26 sales compounded at 11.9%, operating profit at 10.2% and net profit at 9.9%. Operating margin ranged from 23.8% (FY20) to 36.2% (FY15). That blended number hides three very different regimes.

web_blocks.caption: Era table: revenue CAGR, margin range and drivers, FY15 to H1 FY27 (computed by Python from the blind snapshot)
web_blocks.takeaway: The eras are separated by what was being purchased, not by the calendar. In Era 1 MPS was a margin machine without a growth plan. In Era 2 it paid for growth with margin. In Era 3 it repaired the margin and let operating profit compound faster than sales (18.5% against 14.5% a year). In Era 4 it pruned. The net profit CAGR of 26.1% from FY21 to FY25 includes a depressed FY21 base, caused by a 37% tax rate from one-off tax events [14].
rows: Captive-style content services; FY15 QIP cash idle in liquid funds; FY18 sales -8% [6]
Tata Interactive (FY19 +36%, margin 26%); FY20 price cuts and vendor consolidation; FY21 HighWire [12, 14]
eLearning rightsizing around a core-plus-contractor model, AJE in FY25, MPSLabs AI tooling [15, 22]
AJE revenue cut by more than a quarter; Corporate Learning -16.5%; ex-AJE growth 15.4% [19]
Research margin 48.2%; Unbound in the base; Corporate Learning margin about 25% [2]

web_blocks.html: Era 2 has a clean causal chain, thanks to the FY20 and FY21 reports. Tata Interactive lifted FY19 sales by Rs 96 Cr. It dragged margin down because the acquired e-learning business earned only a 4.4% EBITDA margin that year [12]. FY20 then went wrong for reasons management listed with unusual frankness. Journals lost volume to lower-priced vendors in a vendor-consolidation exercise. Two large educational publishers cut offshore prices and held back volumes ahead of a merger, with book-production prices down about 20% on average. A platform customer moved its IT work to its own captive [12]. Currency-adjusted revenue fell 7.8% to Rs 334 Cr. EBITDA fell Rs 11 Cr. FY21 reversed it. HighWire arrived on 1 July 2020 and platforms rose from 16 to 33% of revenue. Sales grew 26.9% even as e-learning fell 24.5% in the pandemic [14].

Era 3's gain is real, and so is its caveat. Operating margin recovered from 25.3% (FY21) to 31.3% (FY23). The e-learning units were restructured around a core-plus-contractor model modelled on Liberate [22]. But FY25's 33% jump needs decomposition. The CFO gave FY26 ex-AJE revenue of Rs 646 Cr, up 15.4% [19]. That implies ex-AJE revenue of about Rs 560 Cr in FY25. From that I compute that AJE supplied roughly 92% of FY25's Rs 182 Cr revenue increase. Underlying growth was about 6%. FY26's 5.7% is the mirror image. AJE shrank 27% (derived the same way) while the rest of the business grew 15.4%. The Chairman's letter says management 'deliberately set down a lower-quality book of business' [1].

Three structural changes ride on top of that cycle. First, the company introduced MPSLabs, its in-house AI and engineering unit. The FY24 report described it as a hub using machine learning, language models and cloud services for content structuring, generation and accessibility checks. It also stated a pivot towards AI-led SaaS revenue [15]. By FY26 the report cites more than 200 AI engineers and over one million manuscripts processed [1]. Second, Vision 2027, set in 2022, fixed the destination at Rs 1,500 Cr of revenue by FY28. The FY25 report called FY25 the halfway point [16]. Third, management reorganised reporting in Q1 FY26 from Content, Platform and eLearning into three segments. These are Research Solutions (60% of FY26 revenue), Education Solutions (27%) and Corporate Learning (13%). All earlier periods were restated [10, 1]. The FY26 report calls the integrated model 'one engine'.

web_blocks.region_era: India and the United States, 1997 to 2008, with 2025 as the endpoint
web_blocks.mechanism: A captive services unit was created by a corporate parent to serve its own back office. In January 2005 it was released to serve outside clients under its own name, and it listed in 2007. The transition mattered less than the pace of non-parent revenue. The unit used the parent as an anchor customer. Meanwhile it built a sales organisation that could win clients the parent did not control.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: GECIS revenue was US$426M in 2004, all from GE. It became independent in January 2005. 2005 revenue was US$493M, of which 85% came from GE and 15% from new clients. It listed on the NYSE in August 2007. Revenue crossed US$1B in 2008 with 53% from non-GE clients. 2025 revenue was US$5.08B (source: Wikipedia company history, citing company and press reports) [23].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: MPS is the same species at a smaller scale and a slower tempo. It was an in-house arm of Macmillan until 2011. Its largest customer today is 17.3% of revenue (Rs 133.17 Cr of Rs 768.37 Cr in FY26) [1]. Genpact took about three years from independence to get more than half of its revenue from outside its parent. MPS, fifteen years after its own ownership change, still has one customer at 17.3% of revenue. Its top five are roughly 45 to 46% [24, 2]. The lesson is not that MPS lacks a moat. The moat is relationship-and-workflow depth, which is slower to scale than a sales force.

web_blocks.caption: Capital returned to shareholders FY19-FY26 (company's own chart) with dividend per share where verifiable
web_blocks.takeaway: Rs 651.22 Cr was returned between FY19 and FY25. I computed this as 56.11 + 93.08 + 41.58 + 155.96 + 34.21 + 128.30 + 141.98. That is about 99% of the Rs 659 Cr of cumulative snapshot net profit over the same years. FY26 broke the pattern. No final dividend was declared because cash went into Unbound Medicine. The FY25 final of Rs 50 a share (Rs 85.53 Cr) was still paid in FY26 [1]. The company's rule is that capital must earn its return within twelve months or go back to shareholders [1]. The FY26 decision shows the rule is discretionary on how 'earning its return' is judged. I found no special dividend or tender offer in the filings I read. The one buyback is the FY22 programme.
rows: Snapshot shows 0%; the company chart is used [16]
Equity capital falls from Rs 18 Cr to Rs 17 Cr [7]
FY25 final of Rs 50 paid in FY26
Cash deployed into Unbound; Rs 42 Cr term loan drawn 6 Feb 2026, repaid August 2026 [1, 2]

web_blocks.html: On leadership continuity the picture is mixed and worth stating plainly. Rahul Arora joined in August 2012 as CMO. He relocated to the United States in early 2013 to set up MPS North America and lead the first acquisition wave. He became CEO and Managing Director afterwards and is now Chairman and CEO combined [1]. His FY26 remuneration was 191 times the median employee and rose 31.33% [1]. The CFO changed on 1 October 2024, when Prarthana Agarwal succeeded Sunit Malhotra, who had joined in 2012 [1, 4]. The Company Secretary resigned in May 2026 [1]. The operating bench has turned over quickly. The voice of Corporate Learning on the calls changed from Archana Jayaraj (to Q1 FY26) to Rodney Beach as President (Q3 FY26) to Soma Bhaduri (from Q4 FY26). Sanjeev Talwar gave his first Education update only in Q1 FY27 [10, 18, 19, 25]. The CEO and CFO are the continuity. The layer under them is not.

Finally, the capital-allocation discipline in the acquisition record deserves a fair test. On the Q2 FY27 call the CEO said, “I would rather miss a deal than overpay” [2]. The record supports that on price. Unbound cost US$16.5M against a revenue run-rate of US$700,000 to US$800,000 a month, which is 1.7 to 2.0 times annual revenue (my arithmetic) [1, 19]. AJE cost Rs 69.67 Cr against Rs 52.48 Cr of FY26 pre-tax profit in AJE LLC alone [15, 1]. The record does not yet support a claim of clean integration. The Liberate goodwill impairment, the AJE revenue contraction and Corporate Learning's slide all sit in the FY26 accounts. The honest reading is disciplined on entry price, still learning on integration.

The chapter title promises the stock's past cycles. The business history above cannot answer that alone, because Pass 1 was written without looking at a price. This addendum was added after the business chapters were locked. The price history was pulled from the daily tape (unadjusted closes; weekly-close swings of 35% or more). The multiples are trailing-year P/E on the last reported fiscal-year EPS from the 10-year table. Data before 2012 is excluded because the Macmillan-era demerger and ownership change distort the series. The pattern is blunt. There were three drawdowns of 50% or more since 2015 (-57.7%, -67.5%, -51.9%). They happened inside a business whose operating cash flow roughly equalled profit every year.

web_blocks.caption: The stock's own cycles since 2015: price swings, the multiple underneath, and the business event that explains each
web_blocks.takeaway: In every leg the multiple moved more than the earnings did. Each multiple is the price over the last reported fiscal-year EPS, so the EPS moves use the same years. Trailing EPS rose 14.3% from FY15 (₹33.00) to FY18 (₹37.71) while the multiple fell from 31.0x to 11.5x. It rose 1.70x from FY19 (₹40.84) to FY24 (₹69.43) while the multiple went from 4.7x to 41.7x. From FY24 to FY25 (₹87.05) it grew 25.4% while the multiple collapsed from 41.7x to 16.0x. FY26 EPS, reported in May 2026, then rose a further 16.3% to ₹101.26. The business compounded steadily. The price paid for that compounding swung by a factor of nine. That is why the entry price, not the business grade, is the decision variable for this stock.
headers: P/E at the end of the leg
rows: FY16 to FY19: sales grew from ₹257 Cr to ₹363 Cr but operating margin slid from 35% to 26% by FY19 (the last step being Tata Interactive's lower-margin e-learning work), and EPS stayed in a ₹38 to ₹41 band (FY15 ₹33.00 to FY18 ₹37.71, +14.3%). The multiple, not the earnings, did the damage.
FY19 sales jumped 36% on the Tata Interactive acquisition (May 2018); the market paid for scale before the margin dilution showed.

The Covid crash on top of FY20's price cuts (about 20% on offshore book work), journal volume lost in a vendor consolidation and a platform customer moving work in-house (FY20 sales -9%, EPS ₹32.15 from ₹40.84). The deepest fall in the table and the cheapest multiple in the ten-year band.

HighWire (July 2020) lifted platform revenue, margin recovered from 25% to 31%, buybacks and large dividends shrank the share count, and AJE drove most of FY25's 33% revenue growth. Trailing EPS rose 1.70x (FY19 ₹40.84 to FY24 ₹69.43). The multiple rose almost nine-fold.

FY26 revenue grew 6% as AJE's clean-up shrank Research, Corporate Learning fell 16.5%, while, in the market's telling, AI worries weighed on content and services names. Trailing EPS still grew 25.4% (FY24 ₹69.43 to FY25 ₹87.05). FY26 EPS, reported in May 2026, rose a further 16.3% to ₹101.26.
Unbound Medicine's first quarters, an FY27 EBITDA floor of ₹300 Cr (May 2026) and Q1 FY27 (+20% revenue, 34% EBITDA margin).
Q2 FY27 revenue +15% and EBITDA +27%, with the FY27 floor raised to ₹310 Cr; reported profit fell 6% only because the prior-year quarter carried a ₹13 Cr one-time gain.

web_blocks.html: Read the table as a statement about the shareholder's experience, not the company's. A holder who bought in April 2015 was down two-thirds at the March 2020 low. That holder did not see the starting price again until 2023. A holder who bought in March 2025 at 41.7x lost half in eleven months while trailing EPS grew 25.4% (FY24 to FY25). Over five years to 12 November 2026 the shares compounded at about 26% a year. Over three years the figure is about 15% a year (price only). Over the last twelve months the return is roughly flat. None of that contradicts the audited record of Chapters 2 to 6. It explains why the same compounder can be a spectacular or a punishing holding, depending only on the entry multiple. Chapters 7 to 9 therefore treat the price as the open question that the business chapters could not settle.

book_paragraphs: Let us begin where the company begins, with a date and an accident of birth. In 1970 a British publishing house, Macmillan, set up an Indian subsidiary whose job was to do for it the work that publishers do not much like doing themselves: the keying, the copy-editing, the page-making, the production-tracking that turns a manuscript into a book. Six years later a former British prime minister, Harold Macmillan, inaugurated the new publishing-services division in Bangalore. Think about what that means for a young services firm. It had a customer before it had a sales team. It had work before it had to win any. For four decades that is what MPS was: a captive, the in-house factory of someone else's brand.

A captive learns things an independent vendor never has to. It learns the publisher's quirks, because its parent is the publisher. It learns quality, because the parent will not forgive a mistake. And it learns, if it is lucky, to be low-cost, because the parent always has an outside quote in the drawer. What it does not learn is how to sell, how to say no to an unprofitable client, or how to put its own capital to work. Keep that thought in mind, because the next fifty years of this story are really the story of a company acquiring, one deal at a time, the skills a captive never needed.

The break came in 2011. A Delhi business-services company, ADI BPO Services, took over Macmillan's stake and with it management control. If you ask who owns MPS today, the answer is still that company: it owns 68.34% of the shares, the same number in every quarter I can see from late 2023 to September 2026. A year after the change of owner a marketer named Rahul Arora joined as Chief Marketing Officer. By early 2013 he was in the United States setting up MPS North America, and the first wave of acquisitions followed within months. Notice how fast the pattern set: new owner, a new executive charged with growth, and within two years a company that had never bought anything was purchasing American content shops.

Then came the first lesson, and it is an uncomfortable one. In the year to March 2015 the company raised about Rs 148 crore from investors in order to do something large. Three years later a trade-press analyst observed that only a sliver of it had been spent on acquisitions and the rest was sitting in liquid funds. You can see it in the numbers. Investments on the balance sheet climbed from Rs 159 crore in FY15 to Rs 288 crore in FY18, while sales fell 8% in FY18, the first decline in the series. Return on capital employed slid from 49% to 23% over those years, not because the business got worse, but because it was carrying a pile of cash. A company that wants to be a consolidator and cannot find anything to consolidate is just a cash pile with a payroll.

So in 2018 MPS did something different and bought a business with a past: Tata Interactive Systems, the e-learning unit of Tata Industries, for up to Rs 80 crore in cash. It came with Rs 140 crore of revenue, close to half the size of MPS itself, and with a margin that, by the company's own account, was 4.4% in the year after it was folded in. Revenue jumped 36% in FY19. Operating margin fell from 33% to 26%. Both happened for the same reason. If you remember only one pair of numbers from this chapter, make it that one: a large, low-margin purchase lifts revenue and drags margin, and the years that follow are a test of whether management can repair what it bought. The 2024 purchase of AJE, which arrived loss-making, would repeat the pattern.

The test came fast, and it did not go well at first. Read what management wrote in its FY20 report, because it is unusually frank. Revenue fell almost 8% and EBITDA fell by Rs 11 crore. The journals business lost volume to lower-priced rivals when a large publisher consolidated its vendors. Two big school publishers cut offshore prices and held work back ahead of a merger; in book production, offshore prices came down by about 20% on average. And one platform customer moved its IT work in-house, to its own captive. Do you see the irony? The thing MPS had been, a captive, was now eating a piece of MPS's own revenue. A year later HighWire Press, acquired on the first of July 2020, lifted platforms from 16 to 33% of revenue and sales rose 27% in a pandemic year, even though e-learning shrank by nearly a quarter and a one-time tax settlement of an old Macmillan-era dispute dented earnings per share.

From FY21 to FY25 something rarer happened. Revenue compounded at 14.5%, operating profit at 18.5% and net profit at 26%, and return on capital employed climbed from 24% to 41%. The new vision, written in 2022 and called Vision 2027, set a destination of Rs 1,500 crore of revenue by FY28, and the acquisition playbook shifted from distressed assets to what management calls growth assets: EI Design in 2022, Liberate Learning in Australia in 2023, and AJE, bought from Springer Nature in February 2024 for about US$8.4 million. The CEO told his Q2 FY25 call that AJE was, in his words, “MPS 2.0”: another business where an obvious fix could be made in months.

Be careful with FY25's 33%, though, because you can break it into pieces. The CFO's figure for FY26 revenue excluding AJE implies that the rest of the business made about Rs 560 crore in FY25, so AJE supplied roughly 92% of that year's Rs 182 crore revenue increase and the underlying growth was nearer 6%. FY26's 6% is the mirror image: AJE shrank by more than a quarter as management deliberately set down a lower-quality book, while the rest of the group grew 15%. Two odd-looking years, one story: an acquisition inflated the base and a clean-up deflated it. By the half-year to September 2026, revenue was Rs 448.5 crore, up 17.8%, and EBITDA was Rs 154 crore at a 34.3% margin, the highest the company has reported. History, then, reads as three acts: captive, collector, and an operator whose edge shows up as margin.

What should you carry out of this history into the chapters that follow? Three things. First, the downturns in this company's life have been price-and-mix events, not demand collapses: a vendor-consolidation round, a customer taking work in-house, a pandemic that froze one segment while another boomed. Second, the upturns have come when management bought an asset it could fix and then fixed it, which means the quality of the integration, not the size of the market, is the variable that matters. Third, one customer still supplies about 17% of revenue and the top five supply roughly 45%, so the loss of a single relationship is the kind of event that moves a year. Keep those three in your pocket; every later chapter either confirms or complicates them.

book_callouts.title: Narrator's reflection: the factory that learned to be chosen
book_callouts.quote: A captive learns to be low-cost; an independent has to learn to be chosen.
book_callouts.text: MPS spent forty years being handed its work. Everything since 2011 has been an apprenticeship in being picked, and in picking: which clients to pursue, which acquisitions to make, and which revenue to turn away. The pattern in the numbers is that the two largest purchases by revenue, Tata Interactive and AJE, pulled margin down and the repairs pushed it back up, which means the right question is never 'did it grow' but 'what did it cost in margin, and was the margin recovered'.
bullets: Margin and growth have rarely been maximised in the same year; H1 FY27 is the first time both are strong together.
Price-and-mix cycles, not volume cycles, have defined the downturns: FY20's offshore price cuts of about 20% are the clearest precedent for AI-era pricing pressure.
The founding captive instinct (reliability, cost discipline, long relationships) survives as the moat; the sales instinct is the newer, still-maturing muscle.

book_subsections.title: The collector's ledger
paragraphs: Let us walk through the purchases the way an accountant would, because the pattern is clearer on paper than in the press releases. Eleven acquisitions in thirteen years is the company's own count. Four deals since 2022 have prices we can read in the audited notes: EI Design for Rs 42 crore, the first 65% of Liberate for Rs 70 crore including amounts deferred, AJE for Rs 70 crore, and Unbound Medicine for Rs 140 crore. Together that is about Rs 322 crore, and the first thing worth noticing is how small it is beside the Rs 460 crore the company returned to shareholders in the four years from FY22 to FY25.

That ratio tells you what kind of acquirer this is. It is not borrowing or issuing shares to grow; it is spending a minority of its cash flow on deals and giving most of the rest back. The price is visible in the balance sheet, though: goodwill stood at Rs 376 crore at March 2026, about 40% of all assets, so the franchise lives or dies on whether those purchases keep earning. Look at how the record stands. AJE's American entity earned Rs 52 crore before tax in FY26 against a purchase price of Rs 70 crore, a fast payback even after its revenue shrank by almost a third. Liberate is the less comfortable case: management wrote back Rs 15.7 crore of the deferred liability when it bought out the founder's remaining stake, and then impaired Rs 12.9 crore of goodwill in the same year.

Unbound is the newest test and the cleanest, because we know its shape: roughly US$8 to 10 million of annual revenue bought for US$16.5 million, a customer base of medical and nursing schools, and a claim from Unbound itself of a 97% annual institutional renewal rate. The CEO's line on the Q2 FY27 call was “I would rather miss a deal than overpay.” On entry price, the record supports him. On integration, the verdict has to wait for a full renewal cycle.

book_subsections.title: Who is at the wheel
paragraphs: Governance questions are the ones investors skip when numbers look good, so let me raise them here. The promoter is a holding company, ADI BPO Services, which owns 68.34% of MPS and, after a vote in August 2026, is in line to be merged into it. The first attempt at that merger, in 2017 and 2018, was withdrawn; a trade-press critic at the time called it a regulatory tidy-up whose cost would fall on MPS. The second attempt passed a shareholder vote with all promoter and institutional votes in favour and a handful of dissenters among the public, but the tribunal's final sanction is not something I have been able to confirm.

On the executive side, Rahul Arora has been the constant since 2012: marketer, then builder of the American business, then CEO, and now Chairman and CEO together. His pay in FY26 was 191 times the median employee's and grew by nearly a third. The CFO changed in October 2024 after twelve years, and the company secretary has resigned. Underneath, the operating bench has moved quickly: three different voices for Corporate Learning on the calls in under a year, and a new head of Education speaking for the first time in August 2026. None of this is a red flag by itself, but it does mean you should ask, quarter by quarter, whether the people who made a promise are the people who must keep it.

book_subsections.title: Where the money went
paragraphs: Close with the cash, because it answers the question every long-term owner eventually asks: what does this company do with what it earns? For seven years to FY25 the answer was to give it back, Rs 651 crore in total, which is about 99% of everything it earned. That included a Rs 105 crore buyback in FY22. The stated rule is simple: capital must earn its return within twelve months, or it returns to shareholders.

FY26 bent the rule. No final dividend was declared, the FY25 final of Rs 50 a share was paid, and the company borrowed Rs 42 crore for the first time in years to help fund Unbound. Six months later the loan was repaid and cash stood at Rs 163 crore with no debt. How should you read that? As a company that has genuinely decided to treat dividends as the residual after growth. That is a defensible stance, but you should know it is a choice, and that the rule as written leaves room for it.

book_subsections.title: The stock's own cycles: why the same company can feel like two different investments
paragraphs: Everything you have read so far treated the company as a business. A share price is a different animal, and it deserves its own paragraph before we leave the history. When I pulled MPS's price history for the first time, I expected a steady staircase to match the steady cash flow. What I found was a roller coaster. Since 2015 the shares have fallen by 57.7%, then 67.5%, then 51.9%, each time while the company kept earning cash.

Look at the two ends of the last cycle. In March 2025 the shares touched about ₹2,898, which was roughly 42 times the profit of the previous fiscal year. Eleven months later they were ₹1,393, about 16 times the profit of the last reported fiscal year (FY25), even though profit per share in that year had grown 25% and the next year, reported in May 2026, added another 16%. Nothing broke inside the factory. What changed was the price investors would pay for a content-services business at a moment when generative AI made everybody ask how long human-edited content production could keep its pricing. Then, in five months, the shares doubled again as the first-quarter numbers arrived.

What should you take from that? Not that the market is crazy, and not that the business is a trading vehicle. Take the narrower lesson that this company's earnings compound at a pace of the mid-teens, while the multiple on those earnings has ranged from under 5 times to over 40 times in ten years. A buyer pays for both. The business chapters tell us the earnings engine is sound; the price chapters will tell us when the multiple is likely to help rather than hurt.
